story_pergunta: At your company, who decides what the AI can promise?

slides.eyebrow: AI ON THE RISE · AI LIABILITY
slides.headline: An AI email said she could pay late. She was evicted anyway.
slides.sub: A customer-facing agent improvised a promise. Who owns it?

slides.headline: A tenant says an AI assistant approved a late rent payment
slides.body: On 8 November, Laura Mack got an email saying paying on November 30 "works." She got an eviction notice on 16 November and was evicted on 19 November. The company has not confirmed her account or whether the assistant could approve extensions.

slides.label: The overdue rent balance at the center of the dispute
slides.sub: Evicted 11 days before the payment date the email appeared to accept.

slides.headline: What I see in companies: nobody defines what the agent may promise
items: The agent answers fast, but no one decides which commitments it is allowed to make
Its answers are not tied to approved data, so it fills gaps with plausible text
When it is unsure, there is no clear handoff to a person who owns the decision

slides.headline: For a building materials store in southern Brazil, I built an agent with hard limits
items: The AI never sees the catalog: search hands 8 results to the model from 13,312 products
Rules: no made-up specs, never reveals stock, never gives discounts
65 out of 65 real customer questions found the right product

slides.headline: Simple that works beats complex that impresses.
slides.body: An agent that talks to customers does not need to be clever about policy. It needs approved data, a short list of things it can commit to, and a human to call when it is unsure. In practice, that is what keeps a helpful answer from becoming a liability.

slides.eyebrow: WANT TO SEE HOW I DID IT?
slides.headline: Comment SDR.
slides.body: I'll send you the step-by-step of this case by DM. I take AI off the drawing board and put it into production, with measured results.

caption:
A North Carolina tenant says an AI assistant approved paying her overdue $3,934.17 rent on November 30. She received an eviction notice on 16 November and was evicted on 19 November. The company has not confirmed her account, or whether the assistant was authorized to approve extensions.

I am not judging the legal outcome. What I see in companies is simpler: an agent talks to customers, and nobody defined what it is allowed to promise. It answers fast, sounds sure, and fills gaps with plausible text.

That is why I build agents with limits. For a building materials store in southern Brazil, I built an AI sales rep on WhatsApp. It never sees the catalog: a simple search answers in milliseconds and hands 8 results to the model. The rules are clear: no made-up specs, never reveals stock, never gives discounts. The whole flow has 9 nodes: one agent and three tools, including calling a human salesperson. 65 out of 65 real customer questions found the right product.

Simple that works beats complex that impresses.

Comment SDR and I'll DM you how I did it.

Sources: drmahfouz.substack.com

meta.tema: Woman evicted after landlord's AI assistant wrongly told her she could delay rent
meta.valor: Simple that works beats complex that impresses.
meta.angulo: A customer-facing agent that improvises policy is a liability, so ground every answer in company-approved data, set hard limits on what it can commit to, and hand off to a human when unsure.
